abstract: Rumination is a cognitive process characterized by repetitive negative thoughts that persist even in the absence of external threats. Although excessive rumination is associated with stress-related mental disorders, the computational mechanisms underlying its persistence and its impact on threat perception remain unclear. Here, we propose a computational framework in which rumination emerges from recursive learning within a world model. Inspired by the social defeat stress (SDS) paradigm in mice, our model assumes that direct experiences of social defeat first establish beliefs about the threat posed by an aggressor. These beliefs subsequently generate internally simulated experiences, which are repeatedly used to update the beliefs themselves. We investigated how this recursive process reshapes threat perception by allowing the rumination gain, a learning rate controlling internal belief updating, to take both positive and negative values. Through numerical simulations and mathematical analysis, we found that positive gains did not simply reinforce acquired threat beliefs, while negative gains did not simply erase them. Instead, both positive and negative gains could generate markedly divergent threat perceptions, with some simulated individuals perceiving severe threats and others perceiving almost none, despite identical initial beliefs and external experiences. These outcomes qualitatively resemble the coexistence of stress-susceptible and resilient mice following SDS. Our findings suggest that rumination is not merely a repetition of past experiences but a self-referential learning process that can transform identical stressful experiences into fundamentally different perceptions of threat.
